learningObjectives: Create Instances to represent the concrete variations of an Attribute.
Apply the Character property (Valid, Invalid, StraightThrough) correctly.
Distinguish Inner and Boundary Position and the StraightThrough restriction.
Use a representative value only when the same expected behavior justifies an equivalence group.

elements.description: An Instance specifies a variation of an Attribute. Create it with Create Instance or Ctrl+N, Ctrl+I; use a unique name. Tosca can also create Instances from entered Attribute values or an XModuleAttribute.

elements.text: Instances live in Instances Collections. Creating the first Instance under an Attribute creates the collection automatically.

bulletPoints: Attribute = the characteristic. Instance = one specific value that characteristic can take.

elements.description: Valid is the default Character: the value fits the business process and no validation error is expected.

Invalid means the input should be rejected. Independent example: a wrong password test passes only if the implemented checks confirm the required rejection, message and absence of a session; the Character label does not itself execute assertions.
StraightThrough identifies a frequently used path with few dependencies and high business risk if it fails. Linear expansion needs this baseline. It is not merely any default Valid value.

elements.text: Use Toggle Character in the TestCase Design dynamic menu or edit Character in Properties. StraightThrough automatically sets Position to Inner, which cannot be changed while that Character is selected.

bulletPoints: Character describes expected input behavior; it does not automatically determine the execution verdict.
Choose StraightThrough for a useful low-dependency, frequently used baseline.

elements.description: Boundary values are at or around an accepted range edge. Independent integer-age example: 0/1 and 99/100 exercise rejection and acceptance around an inclusive 1–99 range; verify the business rule rather than assuming every range has identical boundaries.

Do not assume a boundary defect is permanently impossible after one test. Changes in validation, data conversion or surrounding logic can reintroduce it even when the published range is unchanged. Keep relevant boundary checks in regression according to risk.

Inner values are away from a chosen boundary. Independent grouping example: if all ages 2–98 follow the same business behavior, choose a representative from that group. If additional age thresholds change behavior, split the group instead of treating all inner values as equivalent.

elements.text: Change Position with Toggle Position or Properties. Valid and Invalid Instances can be boundary values; StraightThrough is restricted to Inner.
Group values only when their expected behavior justifies it. Random choice alone does not establish equivalence or replace boundary checks.

bulletPoints: Boundary tests can remain relevant to regression; they are not automatically one-time checks.
Character and Position are separate properties, with the documented StraightThrough/Inner restriction.

examPitfalls.title: Treating an Invalid TestCase result as a failure
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming that if an Invalid Instance produces an error message, the TestCase has failed.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: A negative-input test can pass when its explicit assertions verify the required rejection. Marking an Instance Invalid alone does not implement those checks.

examPitfalls.title: Picking any 'normal' value as the StraightThrough
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Choosing an arbitrary Valid Instance as the StraightThrough without checking dependencies.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Choose the frequently used, low-dependency baseline with high risk if it fails; StraightThrough is required for linear expansion and uses Inner Position.

examPitfalls.title: Testing every value inside a range individually
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Creating a separate Instance for every Inner Value in a large range, e.g. ages 2 through 98.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: First establish equal expected behavior. Then use representative values; split groups at other business thresholds rather than assuming every inner value is equivalent.

examPitfalls.title: Testing only one side of a boundary
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Testing 99 as the upper boundary but skipping 100, or vice versa.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Boundary testing should cover both the last valid value and the first invalid value around each edge (e.g. 99 and 100 for an upper bound of 99), since off-by-one logic errors can occur on either side.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A password test uses an Invalid Instance. All explicit assertions pass: it checks 'Incorrect password' and confirms no session was created. What is the outcome?

options.text: The TestCase fails, because an error occurred.
The TestCase passes, because the expected error behavior occurred.
The result is inconclusive without further data.
Invalid Instances cannot be used for login fields.

practiceQuiz.hint: What does 'Invalid' mean for the Character property, and what should happen when it's applied?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The implemented assertions confirm the expected rejection, so this negative test passes. Invalid Character describes expected input behavior; it does not mark a result failed merely because rejection occurred.

optionExplanations.A: Expected rejection is not failure when all required negative-test assertions pass.
optionExplanations.B: The scenario explicitly says the required assertions passed.
optionExplanations.C: The specified assertions provide the result for this scenario.
optionExplanations.D: Invalid input can be used to test required rejection in login workflows.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which set of criteria correctly describes a StraightThrough Instance?

options.text: Any Instance marked as Valid by default.
Frequently used, with few dependencies and high business risk if it fails.
The Instance with the most dependencies, to maximize test coverage.
Any Boundary Value that is also Invalid.

practiceQuiz.hint: Think 'happy path' — the value most other Attributes can safely be combined with.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The documented StraightThrough path has few dependencies and is most frequently used, making failure high risk. It supplies the baseline for linear expansion and must have Inner Position.

optionExplanations.A: Valid is the default label, not proof that a path is the appropriate baseline.
optionExplanations.B: Frequency, low dependency and business risk match the documented StraightThrough role.
optionExplanations.C: More dependencies make independent variations harder to combine.
optionExplanations.D: StraightThrough must be Inner, so this Invalid Boundary description is not the baseline.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An Attribute accepts ages from 1 to 99. Which four values should be tested as Boundary Values?
practiceQuiz.hint: Boundaries include both the last valid and the first invalid value on each edge of the range.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Boundary testing checks the edges: the value just below the range (0), the first valid value (1), the last valid value (99), and the value just above the range (100) — since off-by-one operator mistakes tend to surface exactly at these points.

optionExplanations.A: 25 and 50 are interior values, not the neighboring values outside these edges.
optionExplanations.B: The two inside/outside pairs exercise the inclusive integer bounds.
optionExplanations.C: The outside rejection cases are missing.
optionExplanations.D: The valid edge acceptance cases are missing.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Business analysis confirms that ages 2–98 all follow the same expected behavior, with no additional thresholds. How can a tester avoid 97 redundant inner-value cases while keeping separate boundary checks?

options.text: Choose a representative from the established equivalence group, and split the group if behavior changes.
Skip testing Inner Values entirely — only Boundaries matter.
Create exactly 10 Instances chosen at random with no further reasoning.

practiceQuiz.hint: A shared expected behavior, not random sampling alone, justifies the group.
practiceQuiz.rationale: For this independently defined scenario, a representative exercises the established common behavior. Additional business thresholds would require separate groups; selection is not a guarantee that all defects are covered.

optionExplanations.A: The stated equal behavior justifies a representative; changed behavior requires another group.
optionExplanations.B: Ignoring all interior behavior does not exercise the equivalence group.
optionExplanations.C: Marking every value StraightThrough does not justify their selection.
optionExplanations.D: Unreasoned random sampling does not establish coverage or equivalence.

quickRecap.value: Attribute variation in an Instances Collection. Create Instance or Ctrl+N, Ctrl+I.
Default Character: value fits the business process.
Rejection expected; explicit checks must verify that outcome.
Frequently used low-dependency baseline, high risk if it fails; requires Inner Position.
Toggle Character / Toggle Position or Properties; StraightThrough automatically sets Inner.
At/around a range edge; retain regression checks according to risk.
Group only values with equivalent expected behavior; split at different business thresholds.
